effect_estimate.comment: All p-values in Tables 1 and 2 are for one-tailed tests. Note that Table 1 labels the final column 'Equation (2.10)' whereas the text refers to 'Equation (1.10)', and in Table 2 Equation (2.6) the unstandardized IMF structural adjustment entry is printed as .038 (SE .007) without significance markers while the text states it is no longer statistically significant.
effect_estimate.value: Water and sanitation access is not modeled as a dependent variable; the dependent variable is infant mortality rate (deaths before age 1 per 1,000 live births; N = 70 observations across 31 countries, one-tailed tests). Higher logged IMF structural adjustment lending per capita is associated with higher infant mortality in baseline two-way FE OLS (Eq. 1.1: b = 0.009, beta = 0.079, robust SE = 0.003, p < 0.01) and two-way FE-IV (Eq. 2.1: b = 0.013, beta = 0.129, SE = 0.006, p < 0.10). Access to an improved water and sanitation source is negatively associated with infant mortality in two-way FE OLS (Eq. 1.2: b = -0.214, beta = -0.231, SE = 0.087, p < 0.01; Eq. 1.3: b = -0.142, beta = -0.153, SE = 0.089, p < 0.10; full model Eq. 2.10/1.10: b = -0.171, beta = -0.185, SE = 0.005, p < 0.05), though statistically non-significant in FE-IV models (Eq. 2.2: b = -0.081, beta = -0.091, SE = 0.145; Eq. 2.6: b = -0.153, beta = -0.171, SE = 0.122). Adding HIV prevalence, access to improved water and sanitation, caloric intake, and immunization rate reduces the IMF structural adjustment coefficient on infant mortality from b = 0.009 (SE = 0.003, p < 0.01) to b = 0.007 (SE = 0.004, p < 0.05) in FE OLS (Eq. 1.3) and from b = 0.013 (SE = 0.006, p < 0.10) to b = 0.012 (SE = 0.007, p < 0.10) in FE-IV (Eq. 2.2), which the authors interpret as partial mediation; no direct regression of water and sanitation access on IMF structural adjustment is reported.

mechanism_certainty.comment: Rated 0 (inferred only). Legal and administrative mechanisms (such as IMF-mandated privatization, subsidy cuts, and higher user fees pricing poor households out of essential services) are posited conceptually in the background narrative and are not measured empirically. Furthermore, the empirical models never directly test an association between IMF structural adjustment (or any legal/institutional variable) and water/sanitation access; combined improved water and sanitation access is entered solely alongside three other health covariates as a predictor of infant mortality, and bivariate correlations are omitted. Design ceiling is also <= 2 due to Serious/Critical ROBINS-I risk of bias.

risk_of_bias_tool.comment: Non-randomized policy/intervention study using two-way fixed effects panel regression and two-way fixed effects instrumental variable (IV) regression to estimate the effect of IMF structural adjustment lending while accounting for time-invariant country heterogeneity and nonrandom policy selection. Overall ROBINS-I risk of bias is Serious/Critical (small sample of 70 observations across 31 countries with unit/period fixed effects and up to 13 covariates, unreported first-stage IV estimates and weak-instrument diagnostics, unestimated exposure-to-mediator regressions, and one-tailed significance tests).
